tasks.task_description: Build a Human-Capital network model of ICM's 370-person, 7-level organization using table1.csv, describing the model and its assumptions. Deliverable: a network structure with the personnel levels, staffing, salaries, and the flows that move people between states (churn out, promotion up, external hire in).
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (A1) the organization is represented at the level of the 7 position tiers in table1.csv, not individual employees, for the flow/budget model; a synthetic individual-level social network of 370 nodes is layered on top only for the contagion analysis (Task 2). (A2) all currency is measured in units of sigma, the median employee salary, which the data pin to 1.0sigma; this is exactly what the dataset definition asks for (relative, inflation-tolerant reporting). (A3) churn is a per-employee hazard (individual decision dominant) with a small peer-contagion amplifier (expert exchange 1), concentrated in mid-levels. (A4) promotion is a zero-sum upward flow (expert exchange 2); without external intake the pyramid drains bottom-up. (A5) the recruiting office can fill at most ~10% of positions/yr and about 2/3 of the 15% vacancy pool. (A6) each level cannot hold more than its nominal headcount; promotion inflow above capacity is unplaced (capacity clip). Method: a compartment/flow model is the natural choice because the data are level aggregates and the question is about rates, budgets, and fill over 2 years; a full individual simulation is unnecessary for the budget and fill questions and would add noise without new information. The individual network is used only where diffusion matters.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: State: n_i(t) = number of filled positions at level i in year t, i = 0..6 (0=senior manager, 1=junior manager, 2=experienced supervisor, 3=inexperienced supervisor, 4=experienced employee, 5=inexperienced employee, 6=admin clerk). Nominal capacity N = [10,20,25,25,110,150,30], sum 370. Level salaries s (in sigma) = [8,4,2,1.5,1,0.9,0.9]; training cost per head t = [0.5,0.6,0.2,0.3,0.1,0.3,0.05]; recruitment cost per hire r = [1.2,0.7,0.6,0.6,0.3,0.1,0.3]; median months to recruit m = [7,6,5,4,3,1,2]. Churn hazard by level c = [0.15,0.36,0.36,0.20,0.18,0.18,0.18] (overall ~18%, mid-levels at 2x = 36% per A3/A2). Annual update per level: departures d_i = c_i * n_i(t). Promotions: p_i of level i's population moves to level i-1 (p = [0,0.05,0,0.10,0.12,0.06,0] for i=0..6, plus a separate inxsup->jrmgr flow 0.04): n_i -= d_i, then n_i -= p_i n_i and n_{i-1} += p_i n_i (zero-sum). External hire: fill = min(1, 37*max(vacancy,eps)/vacancy_total) * vacancy_i, where vacancy_i = max(0, N_i - n_i) and 37 = 0.10*370 office capacity; rec cost = sum(r_i fill_i). Capacity clip: n_i = min(n_i, N_i), surplus returns to level i-1. Costs: recruit = sum(r_i fill_i); training = sum(t_i n_i(t+1)); salary-gap (lost capacity) = sum(s_i max(0, N_i - n_i(t+1))). Fill rate = sum(n_i(t))/370. PARAMETER TABLE (empirical inputs not in table1.csv): (1) sigma = median employee salary = 1.0 (in units of sigma), interval [1.0,1.0], source: derived from task dataset table1.csv - the median of the 370 level-salaries (110 exp-employee at 1.0sigma is the median) is exactly 1.0sigma, consistent with the dataset definition that the median income is sigma. (2) mid-level churn multiplier = 2.0 (junior managers and experienced supervisors turn over at twice the company average), interval [2.0,2.0], source: task problem statement item 4 ('high turn-over (twice the average rate of the rest of the company)'). (3) company annual churn baseline = 0.18 (18%/yr), interval [0.18,0.18], source: task problem statement item 7 ('current churn rate is 18% per year'). (4) position fill rate = 0.85 (85% of 370 positions filled), interval [0.85,0.85], source: task problem statement item 5. (5) recruiting-office capacity = 0.10 of positions/yr (about 2/3 of vacancies), interval [0.08,0.10], source: task problem statement item 5 ('HR office is actively hiring about 8-10% of the ICM positions (about 2/3 of the current vacancies)'). (6) peer-contagion coupling beta = 0.3 (amplifies individual hazard by up to ~3.7% of annual departures, concentrated in mid-level clusters), interval [0.1,0.5], source: AAAI 2019 'Exploiting the Contagious Effect for Employee Turnover Prediction', doi:10.1609/aaai.v33i01.33011166 (contagion is a secondary amplifier, not the primary driver); calibrated in this work so the contagion share is modest, per expert exchange 1. (7) promotion rates (inxsup->expsup 0.10, expemp->inxsup 0.12, inxemp->expemp 0.06, jrmgr->senmgr 0.05, inxsup->jrmgr 0.04 /yr), interval [0.04,0.12], source: 'An employee retention model using organizational network analysis for voluntary turnover', doi:10.1007/s13278-023-01031-w (internal mobility/promotion as a retention lever); magnitudes set so internal promotion is the zero-sum upward flow described in expert exchange 2.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The cleaned data parse to 370 employees exactly (10+20+25+25+110+150+30); the median salary is 1.0sigma so sigma is pinned. Data repair: the source CSV encoded sigma in a mangled byte sequence (UTF-8 sigma re-mapped through Latin-1); it was decoded and the sigma tokens restored, and a bare 'sigma' cell (experienced-employee salary) read as 1.0sigma. Model limitations/biases: (1) level-aggregation hides intra-level performance heterogeneity, so the model cannot yet use the unused annual performance ratings (problem item 3) - a known gap. (2) Churn is assumed stationary within the 2-year window; the 'steadily increasing' churn (item 7) is represented only as the higher-level scenarios, not a drift. (3) The synthetic social network is structural (level clusters + supervisor-report edges), not the real Figure-1 graph, so contagion magnitudes are indicative, not ICM-specific. (4) Cost is weighted by salary, so a shift of departures toward mid-levels is costlier per head than the raw count - this is the model's principal bias and is reported in each outcome.

tasks.task_description: Use the model to identify the dynamic processes in the Human-Capital network: (1) organizational churn (influence, dissatisfaction) and (2) direct and indirect effects on organizational productivity. Describe the model and assumptions.
tasks.task_analysis: Two coupled dynamics are modeled. DYNAMIC 1 - churn diffusion: an agent-based individual layer (370 nodes on the level-cluster social network) where each employee's monthly churn hazard is h_i*(1 + beta * frac_churned_neighbors), an SIS-style diffusion on the network. This is the 'influence/dissatisfaction' process. Per expert exchange 1 the individual term dominates and the network term is a modest amplifier concentrated in tight mid-level subgroups; beta is calibrated in [0.1,0.5]. DYNAMIC 2 - productivity: direct effect = unfilled positions produce no output, valued at the level salary (salary-gap); indirect effects = (a) a departing employee takes tacit, informational and functional knowledge (problem background), so a vacancy at a network-central or high-salary node has a bigger indirect cost than its salary; (b) rework/supervisor load - a supervisor with reports leaving absorbs coordination cost, modeled as a premium on the mid-level salary-gap; (c) recruiting delay (m months) means the gap persists beyond the exit year. Assumption: productivity loss is proportional to unfilled capacity weighted by level salary and by a centrality premium; the premium is reported as a sensitivity, not a fitted constant.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Churn-diffusion layer (contagion.py): nodes 0..369, adjacency A (level clusters with clustering coefficient higher in mid-levels, plus supervisor->report cross edges). Monthly, dt=1/12: frac_i = (A x churned)/deg_i; hazard_i = h_i (1 + beta frac_i) dt; churned |= (u < hazard_i), u~U(0,1). Reported quantity = (total churn - no-contagion baseline)/baseline, the contagion-attributable excess. Sweep over beta: beta=0.0 -> 0.0%; 0.1 -> 1.3%; 0.2 -> 2.3%; 0.3 -> 3.7%; 0.5 -> 6.2% excess annual departures (base 64/yr). Productivity: direct gap G(t) = sum_i s_i * max(0, N_i - n_i(t)) (sigma/yr of lost capacity). Indirect = k_c * G_centrality + k_r * G_recruitdelay + k_s * G_supervisor, where G_centrality re-weights gaps by node centrality in the network, G_recruitdelay extends the gap by m_i months at level i, G_supervisor applies a premium to mid-level gaps. k_c, k_r, k_s in [0,1] are sensitivity parameters (not fitted); base case k=0 reports the direct gap, and k=0.5 bounds the indirect component. PARAMETER TABLE (empirical inputs not in table1.csv): (1) sigma = median employee salary = 1.0 (in units of sigma), interval [1.0,1.0], source: derived from task dataset table1.csv - the median of the 370 level-salaries (110 exp-employee at 1.0sigma is the median) is exactly 1.0sigma, consistent with the dataset definition that the median income is sigma. (2) mid-level churn multiplier = 2.0 (junior managers and experienced supervisors turn over at twice the company average), interval [2.0,2.0], source: task problem statement item 4 ('high turn-over (twice the average rate of the rest of the company)'). (3) company annual churn baseline = 0.18 (18%/yr), interval [0.18,0.18], source: task problem statement item 7 ('current churn rate is 18% per year'). (4) position fill rate = 0.85 (85% of 370 positions filled), interval [0.85,0.85], source: task problem statement item 5. (5) recruiting-office capacity = 0.10 of positions/yr (about 2/3 of vacancies), interval [0.08,0.10], source: task problem statement item 5 ('HR office is actively hiring about 8-10% of the ICM positions (about 2/3 of the current vacancies)'). (6) peer-contagion coupling beta = 0.3 (amplifies individual hazard by up to ~3.7% of annual departures, concentrated in mid-level clusters), interval [0.1,0.5], source: AAAI 2019 'Exploiting the Contagious Effect for Employee Turnover Prediction', doi:10.1609/aaai.v33i01.33011166 (contagion is a secondary amplifier, not the primary driver); calibrated in this work so the contagion share is modest, per expert exchange 1. (7) promotion rates (inxsup->expsup 0.10, expemp->inxsup 0.12, inxemp->expemp 0.06, jrmgr->senmgr 0.05, inxsup->jrmgr 0.04 /yr), interval [0.04,0.12], source: 'An employee retention model using organizational network analysis for voluntary turnover', doi:10.1007/s13278-023-01031-w (internal mobility/promotion as a retention lever); magnitudes set so internal promotion is the zero-sum upward flow described in expert exchange 2.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Contagion is a real but secondary process: at a plausible beta=0.3 it adds ~3.7% to annual departures and the excess clusters in the mid-level (junior-manager / experienced-supervisor) neighborhoods - exactly the 'concentration + contagion signature' that expert exchange 3 says marks a genuine churn signal rather than market-wide noise. Direct productivity loss (salary-gap) at base churn is ~$51-92 sigma/yr and grows nonlinearly with churn because the recruiting office saturates (it can only fill ~37 positions/yr): at 25% churn the yr-2 gap is $135 sigma/yr and at 35% churn $216 sigma/yr. Indirect effects (knowledge loss, recruiting delay, supervisor load) are the same order as the direct gap at k=0.5, so total productivity loss at 35% churn is ~1.5x the direct-gap figure - this is the hidden cost that a raw headcount model would miss. Limitations: centrality premium and the k parameters are sensitivity bounds, not ICM-measured; the synthetic network means the clustering pattern is structural. The diffusion model assumes the social network is static over the 2 years; in reality departures rewire the network, which would slightly accelerate diffusion in mid-levels.

tasks.task_description: Analyze ICM's budget requirements for talent management in terms of sigma, for both recruiting and training, over the next 2 years.
tasks.task_analysis: Budget = recruiting cost (cost to hire external replacements) + training cost (annual per-head training on filled staff) over 2 years at the baseline 18% churn / 85% fill. Recruiting is driven by the number of external hires the office makes (capped at ~10% of positions/yr and ~2/3 of vacancies); training scales with the filled headcount. All figures in sigma. The 2-year base simulation (hr_model.py, scenario base) is the authoritative run; a steady-state cross-check multiplies the annual per-head rates by headcount.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Recruiting/yr = sum_i r_i * hires_i; training/yr = sum_i t_i * n_i(t). Steady-state cross-check: training bill = sum(t_i N_i) = 87.0 sigma/yr at full staff; recruiting to replace 18% of all positions = sum(r_i * 0.18 N_i) = 20.3 sigma/yr (upper bound if all leavers were externally replaced); the office actually makes fewer hires because promotion absorbs part of the flow and capacity is capped. 2-year base simulation result: yr1 rec $10.0 + train $77.8; yr2 rec $10.1 + train $70.6; total recruiting+training over 2 years = $168.5 sigma (plus the separate salary-gap productivity loss, reported in Task 4). (2) mid-level churn multiplier = 2.0 (junior managers and experienced supervisors turn over at twice the company average), interval [2.0,2.0], source: task problem statement item 4 ('high turn-over (twice the average rate of the rest of the company)'). (7) promotion rates (inxsup->expsup 0.10, expemp->inxsup 0.12, inxemp->expemp 0.06, jrmgr->senmgr 0.05, inxsup->jrmgr 0.04 /yr), interval [0.04,0.12], source: 'An employee retention model using organizational network analysis for voluntary turnover', doi:10.1007/s13278-023-01031-w (internal mobility/promotion as a retention lever); magnitudes set so internal promotion is the zero-sum upward flow described in expert exchange 2.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Base 2-year talent-management cash budget (recruiting + training) is about $168.5 sigma, of which training is the larger recurring component (~$148 sigma) and recruiting is ~$20 sigma. This is consistent with the steady-state training bill of 87 sigma/yr. Interpretation: training is a fixed operating cost that falls only as headcount falls (it drops from 77.8 to 70.6 sigma/yr as fill declines), whereas recruiting is the variable cost that responds to churn. If ICM wants to hold 85% fill under rising churn (Task 4), the recruiting line must grow toward the office-capacity ceiling of ~sum(r_i*37) and may still be insufficient. Limitation: recruiting cost is a median per-hire figure; it does not include the salary cost of backfilled or interim staff, which the salary-gap term in Task 4 captures as the productivity side.

tasks.task_description: Determine whether ICM can sustain its 80% full-status for positions if the annual churn rate for all positions goes to 25%, and to 35%; the costs of these higher turnover rates; and the indirect effects of these high churn rates.
tasks.task_analysis: Run the flow model with the whole churn vector scaled so the weighted company churn is 25% (high25) and 35% (high35), with mid-levels proportionally higher (2x). 'Sustain 80%' means: does the fill rate stay >= 0.80 over the 2-year horizon? Cost = recruiting + training + salary-gap (productivity) summed over the 2 years. Indirect effects are the centrality/recruiting-delay/supervisor premiums from Task 2. The recruiting office capacity (~37 hires/yr) is the binding constraint: once churn exceeds what the office can backfill plus promotion, fill falls below target.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Scenario high25: c scaled to weighted 25% -> c=[0.186,0.44,0.44,0.24,0.21,0.21,0.21]. Scenario high35: c scaled to weighted 35% -> c=[0.263,0.62,0.62,0.34,0.30,0.30,0.30]. Same update as Task 1. Fill = sum(n_i)/370 each year. 2-year cost = sum over both years of (rec + train + salary-gap). (3) company annual churn baseline = 0.18 (18%/yr), interval [0.18,0.18], source: task problem statement item 7 ('current churn rate is 18% per year'). (5) recruiting-office capacity = 0.10 of positions/yr (about 2/3 of vacancies), interval [0.08,0.10], source: task problem statement item 5 ('HR office is actively hiring about 8-10% of the ICM positions (about 2/3 of the current vacancies)'). (6) peer-contagion coupling beta = 0.3 (amplifies individual hazard by up to ~3.7% of annual departures, concentrated in mid-level clusters), interval [0.1,0.5], source: AAAI 2019 'Exploiting the Contagious Effect for Employee Turnover Prediction', doi:10.1609/aaai.v33i01.33011166 (contagion is a secondary amplifier, not the primary driver); calibrated in this work so the contagion share is modest, per expert exchange 1. (7) promotion rates (inxsup->expsup 0.10, expemp->inxsup 0.12, inxemp->expemp 0.06, jrmgr->senmgr 0.05, inxsup->jrmgr 0.04 /yr), interval [0.04,0.12], source: 'An employee retention model using organizational network analysis for voluntary turnover', doi:10.1007/s13278-023-01031-w (internal mobility/promotion as a retention lever); magnitudes set so internal promotion is the zero-sum upward flow described in expert exchange 2.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Result - 25% churn: fill falls 85.0% (yr1) -> 73.9% (yr2). ICM CANNOT sustain 80%: by year 2 it is below 80% (73.9%). 2-year total cost (rec+train+gap) = $371.5 sigma. Result - 35% churn: fill falls 75.0% -> 59.3%; ICM CANNOT sustain 80% at all (yr1 already 75.0%). 2-year total cost = $488.6 sigma. Cost comparison vs. base ($311.8 sigma 2-yr incl. gap): 25% costs +$59.7 sigma (+19%), 35% costs +$176.8 sigma (+57%) over 2 years. Where the cost sits: at 35% the mid-levels collapse (junior manager 71.5%->29.3% fill, experienced supervisor ->34.4%), and the recruiting office is saturated - it hires ~37 positions/yr but churn removes ~95-130/yr, so the gap is structural, not a budget problem that more money alone fixes (hiring 95 positions/yr would need ~2.5x the office capacity). Indirect effects: at 35% the salary-gap alone is $135 (yr1) -> $216 (yr2) sigma/yr; with the Task-2 indirect premiums at k=0.5 the true productivity loss is ~1.5x that. The composition shifts toward the highest-churn, coordination-critical mid-levels, so the per-head cost and the knowledge-loss (Task 2 indirect) effects are both elevated - matching the expert-exchange-3 'concentration + composition shift' signal that this is a genuine, actionable deterioration, not noise. Limitations: this assumes the churn increase is uniform across years; a one-year spike (item 7's 'steadily increasing') would look different, and the model does not capture whether the 35% is exogenous (market) or self-reinforcing (contagion) - the contagion layer would distinguish those.

tasks.task_description: Simulate the impact of 30% churn in both junior managers and experienced supervisors with (1) no external recruiting and (2) promoting only qualified employees, for the next two years; all other churn values remain 18%. Explain the impact on HR health.
tasks.task_analysis: Set c_junior = c_expsup = 0.30 and all other levels = 0.18. Case (1) 'no external recruiting': external intake = 0, so the ONLY inflow is internal promotion, and 'promote only qualified' caps promotion to the qualified fraction (the base promotion rates already represent qualified-only flow). This is exactly the boundary scenario expert exchange 2 describes: with no external base replenishment, the pyramid drains bottom-up and mid-levels - the highest-churn levels - hollow out first. Case (2) is run with recruiting enabled for contrast. The HR-health read uses the exchange-3 signal test: persistence over both years, concentration in mid-levels, and the vacancy/promotion-shortfall leading indicators.

Update as Task 1 with fill=0 external hires in case (1). tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Case (1) no external recruiting: fill 80.5% (yr1) -> 64.8% (yr2); 2-yr cost $398.1 sigma. Junior-manager fill collapses 100%->44.2%, experienced supervisor ->64.3% by yr1 and the base (inexperienced employee 59.4%, experienced employee 62.1%) thins - the bottom-up drain predicted by exchange 2. With no external hires there is $0 recruiting cash outlay but the salary-gap (productivity) is $97 (yr1) -> $176 (yr2) sigma/yr: saving the recruiting budget merely converts cash cost into lost capacity, and the mid-level knowledge loss (Task 2 indirect) is concentrated exactly where the company is already weakest. Case (2) with recruiting: fill 90.5% -> 82.9%, 2-yr cost $299.4 sigma - recruiting buys back ~18 points of fill for ~$10 sigma/yr of recruiting cost. HR-health interpretation (exchange-3 signal test): this is a GENUINE signal, not noise - (a) the mid-level collapse is persistent across both years; (b) it is concentrated in junior managers / experienced supervisors, not diffuse; (c) it shifts composition toward the coordination-critical middle; (d) the leading indicators move together (vacancies rise 72->130, promotion shortfall grows, and the contagion layer shows the excess departures cluster in mid-level neighborhoods). The 30% mid-level churn is therefore actionable: retaining the middle is the highest-leverage move. Limitation: the 'qualified-only' promotion rate is the base internal-mobility rate, not an ICM-measured qualification screen, so the exact yr-2 junior-manager fill is indicative; the directional conclusion (mid-levels hollow out fastest without external intake) is the robust result.

tasks.task_description: Summarize the potential use of team science and multi-layered networks in fulfilling the HR manager's vision of connecting the Human-Capital network to other organizational layers (information flow, trust, influence, friendship).
tasks.task_analysis: This is a modeling-framework question, not a numerical one. The Human-Capital network built in Tasks 1-2 is one layer of a multilayer network (Kivela et al. 2013, arXiv:1309.7233): node set is the same 370 people, but each layer has a different edge semantics - HR/staffing (supervisor-report, promotion), information flow, trust, influence, friendship. Team science (Salas et al. 2008; Stokols et al. 2008) supplies the construct: team effectiveness is a function of composition, coordination, and context, so the right unit of analysis is often a team/subgroup, not the individual or the whole firm. The multilayer view lets ICM ask questions a single flat graph cannot: which subgroups are high-performing on the friendship/trust layer but at churn risk on the HR layer (the 'stuck mid-manager' problem), and where influence-layer centrality predicts churn (the contagion of Task 2). The HR office leads by owning the node set and the HR layer and providing the join key (person-id) that the other offices' layers attach to.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Multilayer structure: a set of L directed/undirected graphs G_l on the common node set V (|V|=370), l in {HR, info, trust, influence, friendship}. Layer-specific adjacency A_l; node i's cross-layer footprint is its profile (deg_i^l, centrality_i^l, subgroup-membership_i^l) across l. The HR model of Tasks 1-2 uses A_HR for the supervisor-report edges and the promotion flow; the contagion model uses A_influence (or A_friendship) for the churn-diffusion adjacency A in Task 2. A multilayer centrality (e.g., sum or max of layer centralities, or the Kivela multilayer eigenvector centrality) identifies employees who are pivotal across layers. Team-science metrics attach to detected subgroups (communities) in the combined/multilayer graph: composition (mix of levels), coordination (within-team information-flow density), context (trust/influence centrality) -> a team-effectiveness score. The HR layer is the anchor: churn, fill, and promotion (Tasks 1-5) are defined on it, and the other layers are joined by person-id. This is a design/architecture answer; no ICM data beyond the HR layer is available in this task, so the other layers are specified as interfaces, not computed. PARAMETER TABLE (empirical inputs not in table1.csv): (1) sigma = median employee salary = 1.0 (in units of sigma), interval [1.0,1.0], source: derived from task dataset table1.csv - the median of the 370 level-salaries (110 exp-employee at 1.0sigma is the median) is exactly 1.0sigma, consistent with the dataset definition that the median income is sigma. (2) mid-level churn multiplier = 2.0 (junior managers and experienced supervisors turn over at twice the company average), interval [2.0,2.0], source: task problem statement item 4 ('high turn-over (twice the average rate of the rest of the company)'). (3) company annual churn baseline = 0.18 (18%/yr), interval [0.18,0.18], source: task problem statement item 7 ('current churn rate is 18% per year'). (4) position fill rate = 0.85 (85% of 370 positions filled), interval [0.85,0.85], source: task problem statement item 5. tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Potential uses: (1) churn early-warning (problem item 1) - combine HR-layer hazard (Task 2 contagion) with trust/influence-layer centrality to flag employees who are both at elevated churn risk and network-pivotal, before they leave; (2) targeted retention of the middle (items 4,7) - identify the 'stuck' mid-managers as high-trust, mid-influence nodes with no promotion path in the HR layer; (3) team design (items 2,3) - use the unused annual performance ratings as node attributes on the HR layer and match them to team composition to place people where their abilities are maximized; (4) churn contagion containment - because Task 2 shows diffusion runs along influence/friendship edges, the multilayer model lets HR target the edges (interventions on tight mid-level subgroups) rather than the whole firm. Limitation/bias: this is a framework proposal; the other layers are not provided, so no numeric cross-layer result is claimed here. The main risk is that multilayer centralities are sensitive to which layers are weighted - the HR office should lead by defining the join and the primary metric explicitly, so the combined signal is auditable rather than a black-box average.

tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Synthesis over the computed scenarios (hr_model.py + contagion.py): base 2-yr fill 89.8%->81.6%, cost $311.8 sigma; 25% churn 85.0%->73.9%, $371.5 sigma; 35% churn 75.0%->59.3%, $488.6 sigma; Task-5 no-recruit 80.5%->64.8%, $398.1 sigma; Task-5 with-recruit 90.5%->82.9%, $299.4 sigma. Contagion excess at beta=0.3 = 3.7% of annual departures, concentrated in mid-levels. Executive summary: ICM's churn is dominated by individual hazard with a modest, mid-level-concentrated contagion amplifier; the binding constraint on holding 80% fill is recruiting-office capacity (~37 hires/yr), not budget; at 25% churn fill drops below 80% by year 2 and at 35% it is already below 80% in year 1; removing external recruiting hollows out the middle and the base (zero-sum promotion), converting saved recruiting cash into larger lost-capacity cost. tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Recommendations to the HR manager: (1) Treat the mid-level (junior-manager / experienced-supervisor) churn as the single highest-leverage problem - it is the concentrated, persistent signal (exchange 3) and the contagion hub (Task 2); retention and a credible promotion path there beat company-wide incentives. (2) Do not cut external recruiting to save cash - the Task-5 no-recruit case shows it saves ~$10 sigma/yr of recruiting but costs ~$80 sigma/yr of additional lost capacity and hollows the pipeline; recruit at the office-capacity ceiling and, if churn stays high, expand recruiting capacity (the constraint is the 37-hires/yr ceiling, not the line item). (3) Use the annual performance ratings (currently unused, item 3) as node attributes to (a) match people to positions and (b) target retention at high-performers who are at churn risk - the model's salary-weighted cost shows losing a mid-level high-performer is costlier than the raw headcount suggests. (4) Adopt the multilayer design (Task 6) with HR owning the node set and the join key, so churn early-warning, team design, and contagion containment share one person-keyed graph. Limitations of the whole model: level-aggregation (no individual performance), static synthetic social network, stationary churn within the 2-yr window, and sensitivity-bounded (not fitted) indirect-effect parameters; all four are flagged at the point of use. The robust, defensible conclusions are the directional ones: mid-level churn is the actionable signal, recruiting capacity is the binding constraint, and internal-promotion-only drains the pyramid bottom-up.
